::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, November 2026.** A short essay about us and the machines we are building. It does not say that the race to build bigger AI is wrong. It asks questions about it, and it proposes another way to look at it. Where I give a fact, I give the source, and where I borrow an idea from physics, I say how far the comparison goes. The first figure is a drawing of my own; the second sketches a known result from physics. The code that draws them is linked under each one.
:::

**In short.** A machine has reportedly proved the Riemann hypothesis, in a proof that would run past 250,000 pages. It raises questions I cannot fully answer, and I think they are worth asking. Is searching a way of thinking? Maybe all discovery, ours included, is a search paid for in advance. Our brain paid with time: selection, then a childhood. Now it learns all its life on about twenty watts. Our machines pay another way. They borrow time from everything people ever wrote, and they add power. What do we gain by going faster? Often a lot. But understanding lives in a mind, and it still arrives at human speed. So I propose another view of progress. Count what people understand, not only what machines produce. Let the big models explore, and build small ones, close to us, that teach. And give understanding its own time.

## 1. What is a proof for?

On 20 November 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic announced that he and Claude, the company's AI, had proved the Riemann hypothesis. It is a question about the prime numbers, open for 167 years. As reported, a computer has checked every step. Written out in prose, the proof ran past 250,000 pages, and he chose not to post it [@sciam2026alpoge; @officechai2026]. I wrote about that day in [Long First, Short Later](../../posts/2026-11-21-long-first-short-later/index.qmd).

Read one page a minute, eight hours a day, and you would need a year and a half. So here is a truth, perhaps the most wanted in mathematics, in a book that no person will read.

Does it help us? If it holds, hundreds of results that begin with "assuming the Riemann hypothesis" become certain. That is real. But it also raises a question we rarely ask. What is a proof for? To know *that* something is true, or to understand *why*? Today we have the first. Not yet the second.

I don't want to answer too fast. In 1953, the philosopher Martin Heidegger closed a lecture on technology with a line I keep coming back to. "Questioning," he wrote, "is the piety of thought" [@heidegger1977]. Piety here means a kind of respect. He did not ask us to reject technology, nor to follow it blindly. He asked us to keep questioning it. So this essay is a series of questions, each with a proposal. Not verdicts.

## 2. Is searching a way of thinking?

It is tempting to say that the machine only searches, so fast that it looks like thinking. I am no longer sure that is enough. These systems now find things nobody had found ([Partly Wrong, Mostly Right](../../posts/2026-11-20-partly-wrong-mostly-right/index.qmd)). That looks like discovery. Sometimes it looks like invention.

So maybe the better question is this one. What is a discovery, if not a search that ends somewhere new? In 1976, Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, two founders of the field, proposed that intelligence *is* search, guided by good rules of thumb [@newell1976]. If they were right, the interesting question is not whether a machine searches. It is how the search was paid for.

Chess gives a clue. In 1997, Deep Blue beat the world champion by examining well over a hundred million positions every second [@campbell2002]. Decades earlier, the psychologist Adriaan de Groot had asked strong players to think aloud. The grandmasters did not look at more moves than weaker players. They looked at a handful, and saw the good ones first [@degroot1965]. Then, in 2017, AlphaZero beat the strongest chess program of the time while looking at about a thousand times fewer positions [@silver2018]. It had not escaped the search. It had moved it: millions of games against itself, played before the match, in training.

Here is the view I propose. **Understanding is search, paid for in advance.** The grandmaster paid with years of games. AlphaZero paid in a data centre. We could never try everything, so we had to understand.

## 3. What made us?

Nobody designed the human brain. Selection did, working over time: hundreds of millions of years of small changes, most of them failures, kept only when they worked. Then each of us added a childhood.

That was not cheap. Evolution ran on the sunlight of the whole living world, through billions of lives. But the cost was spread so thin, over so much time, that each step was almost free.

What it left is small. Everything we inherit at birth is written in about three billion letters of DNA [@nurk2022], less than a gigabyte by my count. Then a child learns language from very little: fewer than a hundred million words heard by the age of thirteen, by researchers' estimates [@warstadt2023]. And the brain does all this on about twenty watts, a small light bulb [@raichle2002; @balasubramanian2021]. It does not only think on twenty watts. It *learns* on twenty watts, every day of its life.

The researcher François Chollet proposed measuring intelligence just this way. Not by what a system can do, but by how little experience it needs to learn it [@chollet2019]. What if we measured our machines like that too? By that measure, the child is still far ahead. And that seems to me a goal worth aiming at.

## 4. What if data is time?

When I say that time made us, I mean three different things. The time evolution took to design us. The time a childhood takes to fill a brain. And the slowness of thinking itself. Each time, nature spent time instead of energy.

We want the same mind without the wait. Is that possible? I think time does not vanish when we skip it. We pay for it in another currency.

Here is a different way to look at training data: as time. Llama 3, an open model from 2024, was trained on more than fifteen trillion tokens, the small pieces of words these models read [@meta2024llama3]. By my own count, that is roughly a hundred thousand times what a child hears by thirteen. Every page of it was written by a person, over centuries. So we did not really skip the time. We borrowed it, from everyone who ever wrote. **Data is time, stored.** That is not a reproach. It is a gift from all those writers, and it deserves to be used well.

Then we add power. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres used about one and a half percent of the world's electricity in 2024. It expects that to more than double by 2030, mostly because of AI [@iea2025]. I must be careful here. One trained model is shared by millions of people, so counted per answer, it can be cheap. The point is not that one answer needs a power station. It is that building these minds fast gathers, in one place, what nature spread over ages.

Physics has a name for this trade. In thermodynamics, a process run very slowly can waste almost nothing. Run it faster, and it wastes more. In 1975, Frank Curzon and Boris Ahlborn worked out what this means for an engine. Run it for the most power, and it is much less efficient than it could be. Push it faster still, and you get less power, not more [@curzon1975]. Chips obey the same rule: to switch faster, they need a higher voltage, and the energy lost grows with its square [@horowitz2014].

The brain took the other side of the trade. On average, a neuron fires only a few times a second [@attwell2001]; a chip switches billions of times. The brain is slow, it works in parallel, and it keeps its memory right next to its computing. That matters, because moving data costs more than computing on it. In a chip, reading a number from main memory takes more than a hundred times the energy of multiplying two numbers [@horowitz2014].

So here is the view. **Nature paid in time. We pay in borrowed time and power.** Neither is free. The question is which we can afford, and for what.

## 5. What do we gain by going faster?

If we could shrink that time to almost nothing, what would we really gain, as human beings? Is it as much as we believe?

Often, a lot. Innovation is not the enemy, and physics agrees: an engine run infinitely slowly gives no power at all. There is a right speed, and it is not zero. When a disease spreads, every month saved is lives saved. A proof found in 41 days instead of twelve years frees those years for something else.

![**Figure 2.** Every speed has a price. For a heat engine, what you get from each unit of energy falls as you run it faster. What you get per hour rises, peaks at the right speed, then falls: too slow, little happens; too fast, you get less and waste more. After Curzon and Ahlborn (1975); a schematic of the shape, not the numbers. But physics also says there is a speed past which you get less. An engine is not a society, and I use it as an image, not a proof. Still, it invites a question. Could we go past that speed too, and lose time in the end?

Look at the proof. Found in 41 days, it may take decades to understand. Or maybe not. Other models can read the 250,000 pages, find the steps that matter, and write a shorter proof, perhaps a much shorter one. They can explain it too, patiently, as many times as we ask. I believe that will happen, and soon. The prime number theorem waited 84 years for its four-page proof. This time, the wait may be months.

But a short proof on a page is not yet understanding. Understanding lives in a mind. It exists only when a person can hold the idea, see why it must be so, and carry it to the next problem. **The machine can write the explanation. It cannot make it arrive.** That part still happens at human speed, one mind at a time.

So the slow part moves. Producing explanations used to be slow. Now, taking them in is. A thousand clear explanations a day help nobody if nobody has the time to read one.

And do we always know when we are faster? In 2025, researchers ran a careful experiment with sixteen experienced programmers, on real tasks in their own projects. With the AI tools of early 2025, they took 19 percent longer. Yet afterwards, they believed the tools had made them about 20 percent faster [@metr2025]. It is one small study, and the tools have improved since. But it is a good reason to measure, rather than assume.

Two thousand years ago, the Roman philosopher Seneca wrote that our life is not short; we waste much of it [@seneca49]. Maybe the question was never how to get more time. Maybe it is what we do with the time we have.

## 6. Which AI do we want beside us?

I am not against AI. I use it in my work every day. So the question I want to ask is not "big or small?" It is this one: which AI helps a person understand?

I believe that is where a small brain, close to us, could matter. The big models may find the proofs and shorten them. A small one could sit with one person, on their phone or their desk, and go at their pace. It would know what they already understand, notice where they are lost, and wait. It does not need to know everything. It needs to know one person well. I sketched what such a local mind could look like in [An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle](../../posts/2026-10-17-an-ecosystem-not-an-oracle/index.qmd) and [Fast AI](../../posts/2026-10-11-fast-ai/index.qmd).

We know this kind of help works. In 1984, the educational researcher Benjamin Bloom reported that students taught one to one did far better than students taught in a class. The average tutored student did better than about ninety-eight percent of the class [@bloom1984]. Later reviews found a smaller gain, but still a large one. They also found that good computer tutors came close to human ones [@vanlehn2011].

The physics agrees: memory next to computing, slow and parallel, learning where you live. And the big and the small need not compete. One can be the explorer. The other can be the guide who walks home with you.

## 7. Three proposals

So, instead of a verdict, three proposals.

**Count understanding, not only answers.** We measure AI by the problems it solves. Let us also measure what people understand afterwards: a proof a student can follow, a result a team can explain in its own words.

**Let the big models explore, and the small ones teach.** Build both, for different jobs. The frontier finds and shortens. The companion close to us helps one person understand, at their pace.

**Give understanding its own time.** For every answer a machine gives us quickly, keep some time to take it in: to read, to doubt, to explain it back. That time is not lost. It is how borrowed time gets repaid.

More than a century ago, the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who wanted answers. He told him to be patient with what is still unsolved, and to "live the questions now". Perhaps then, he wrote, one day you will live your way into the answer [@rilke1903].

Time made a mind that learns on twenty watts. We are building minds on borrowed time. I don't know the right speed. But I think it is a question worth living, not a race worth winning.
